div.head: The improvement of system reliability can be achieved through the use of time redundancy techniques including retry, checkpointing and recovety block. The objective of this paper is to analyze the worst case timing requirement of real-time tasks with time redundancy in the presence of multiple transient faults. The timing behavior of system level checkpointing is modeled with additional tasks that save the state of all tasks. The timing information derived in this paper makes time redundancy techniques applicable to real-time systems while keeping the validity of schedulability check developed in the past.
Introduction
div.p: WCET (Worst Case Execution Time) of real-time tasks is an important metric that is commonly used to guarantee their schedulability. When a fault occurs, extra time is required to handle fault detection and recovery, and it must be accounted for prior to the execution of tasks. There are some scheduling policies developed to ensure that faults are tolerated by incorporating time redundancy [ 1, 5, 6, 71. These approaches, hcwever, lack consideration on various fault tolerance techniques including time redundancy and recovery measures. In this paper, we predict the worst case timing behaviors of real-time tasks with time redundancy, which make those applicable to well-known schedulability check methods. We treat retry, checkpointing, and recovery block as time redundancy techniques, and classify checkpointing into two types of implementation levels as follows:
User level: Checkpointing routines are provided to tasks as a form of library routines [3] or user program routines.

div.head: System level:
div.p: Checkpointing is performed by the operating system. Checkpointing routines are provided as system service similar to process scheduling. This routine is invoked within the system and executed at kernel level to checkpoint states of all running tasks.

We consider only transient and intermittent faults that affect a task during sufficiently short time. It is assumed that faults are detected immediately upon their occurrence by using fault detection mechanisms, and that a program can fail at an arbitrary instant. div.head: System Level Checkpointing
div.p: We assume that the system level checkpointing operates under periodic checkpoint placement strategy where T represents checkpoint interval. Checkpointing system service is periodically executed in order to checkpoint states of all tasks. These behaviors of checkpointing are similar to those of the periodic real-time task; the task which is released every T time units has computational requirement as much as the checkpointing overhead multiplied by the number of tasks. Since it preempts all running tasks, the run-time overhead for system level checkpointing can be predicted through simple scheme. It incorporates a periodic task which is referred to as checkpoint server which performs checkpointing. Fault detection and rollback to the latest checkpoint can be modeled as interrupt that requires constant service time R . Therefore, the worst case rollback and reprocessing time becomes ki . ( R + T + n . C) in the presence of ki faults. But, the simple scheme has a major drawback, priority inversion, in a priority-based system because of the delay of the execution of higher priority tasks caused by check-pointing for lower priority tasks [4]. To avoid the priority inversion, all the tasks that are more urgent than the task under checkpointing must be made to complete before checkpointing is initiated. Therefore, it is sufficient that the checkpointing server saves only the state of a running task. The computational requirement of checkpointing server is reduced to C while its period is T . Its priority must be higher than that of task under checkpointing and lower than that of more urgent tasks. In this priority-based scheme, the worst case rollback and reprocessing time amounts to k; . (R + T + C) in the presence of ki failures.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We now describe how to check the schedulability of tasks which are aided by time redundancy techniques to tolerate faults. It is assumed that system is susceptible to at most k faults during the time interval [O,t,'] and that a task set is composed of N real-time tasks.

In case that system level checkpointing is used, the schedulability of a task set can be checked through the simple scheme addressed in Section 2.4, the introduction of an additional periodic checkpointing server. Furthermore, we provided a modified scheme to avoid priority inversion that can happen in priority-based systems. We now illustrate how the timing information is applicable to schedulability check by C T (Completion Time) test of Lehoczky [ 2 ] , a representative schedulability test in real-time system, although our work is not restricted to rate monotonic scheduling policy. This result shows that equidistant is not optimal checkpoint placement strategy in real-time systems.
